# Week 7: Second-order CFA {.unnumbered}

::: {.week-meta}
Core reading
: @byrne2016, chapter 5, the analysis based on continuous data, pp. 149–162 (about 60 minutes)

Data
: [Student Life Survey](../course/dataset.qmd), clean file

App
: Identification and degrees of freedom

Task style
: Completion: reproduce, then make and justify a decision yourself

:::

## By the end of this week you can

- Specify a higher-order factor in Amos.
- Explain the identification of the higher-order part.
- Decide whether a second-order model is justified.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. What does AVE measure?
2. What does a modification index estimate? (Week 4)

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. The average proportion of variance in a factor's items explained by the factor.
2. How much χ² would fall if one fixed parameter were freed.

</details>

## This week in brief

A second-order factor explains the correlations among first-order factors. It is more parsimonious than letting all first-order factors correlate, but with only three first-order factors the two models fit identically, and with two the higher-order part is not identified.

## In the session

- Specifying a higher-order factor and setting its scale.
- Identification of the higher-order part, with the app.
- Comparing the second-order and correlated-factors models.

## After the session

Read the core reading with these questions in mind:

- Why does Byrne propose a second-order factor for these data (pp. 150–152)?
- With only three first-order factors, why is the upper level of the model just-identified (pp. 153–154)?
- How does she use Amos's critical ratios for differences to choose an equality constraint that resolves this?

## Your task this week

1. Reproduce Byrne's second-order model.
2. Some researchers would argue that support, self-efficacy and engagement reflect a broader "academic adjustment". Fit a second-order factor for those three factors and compare it with the model in which they simply correlate.
3. **Decide:** is the second-order model justified? Use the df, the fit and the theory.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. When is a second-order model just a re-expression of the correlated first-order model?
2. What would justify a second-order factor?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. With three first-order factors the higher-order part is just-identified: three loadings replace three correlations, so df and fit are identical.
2. A theory that the first-order factors are facets of one broader construct, and enough first-order factors (four or more) for the claim to be testable.

</details>

## Checkpoint

You have now finished the single-group measurement weeks.

- [ ] I can specify, fit and evaluate a CFA in Amos.
- [ ] I can find and judge local misfit with residuals and modification indices.
- [ ] I can justify each change to a measurement model.
- [ ] I can report CR, AVE and HTMT for each factor.
- [ ] I can explain when a second-order model is testable.

Anything you cannot yet tick is the first item for the next session.
